description: In sys/kern/tty.c, tty_drop_ctty() clears the session→tty pointers and decrements the refcount but never clears tp->t_session; because s_ttyp is already NULL, sess_release() skips tty_rel_sess(), so when the session struct is freed tp->t_session is left dangling. Closing the pty master later walks tty_rel_gone → ttydisc_modem → tty_signal_sessleader, which dereferences tp->t_session->s_leader and ultimately calls knote() on a klist inside that pointer — an attacker-controllable indirect call. Separately, pmap_pkru_update_range() in sys/amd64/amd64/pmap.c checks X86_PG_V but not PG_PS on PDPEs, so a 1GB SHM_LARGEPAGE mapping causes the kernel to treat a gigabyte of user data as page-table entries, yielding an arbitrary-physical-page read/partial-write and an address oracle for the user page's DMAP kernel VA. Chaining the two gives a nobody-level local attacker a known-address gigabyte of controlled kernel-visible memory plus a control-flow hijack, demonstrated end-to-end to uid=0 on stock 14.4-RELEASE.
location: tty_drop_ctty() in sys/kern/tty.c; pmap_pkru_update_range() in sys/amd64/amd64/pmap.c
reproduction: 1. (Oracle) shm_open2(SHM_ANON, …, SHM_LARGEPAGE) with lp_psind=2, ftruncate to 1GB, mmap at a 1GB-aligned VA; write a fake PDE and sentinel into the page; call sysarch(AMD64_SET_PKRU) on a 4KB sub-range and probe candidate physical bases until the sentinel's bits [62:59] change, revealing the page's physical address and thus its DMAP kernel VA.
2. Build fake struct proc / knlist / knote / filterops and a ROP stack inside the 1GB page at the now-known kernel virtual address.
3. posix_openpt() for a pty master, open the slave, clear CLOCAL on the slave.
4. Fork; child does setsid(), re-opens the slave, ioctl(TIOCSCTTY), ioctl(TIOCNOTTY), _exit(0) — freeing the session while tp->t_session still points at it.
5. Refill the freed malloc-128 session slot (AF_UNIX bind() with a sized sockaddr_un, raced against the close on a second CPU) so that the bytes at offset 8 (s_leader) point to the fake proc.

6. Close the pty master: ttydev_close → tty_rel_gone → ttydisc_modem(tp,0) → tty_signal_sessleader → dereference stale tp->t_session->s_leader → PROC_LOCK → kern_psignal → tdsendsignal → knote(p->p_klist,…) → attacker-controlled kn->kn_fop->f_event(kn,…) → stack pivot → ROP → root.
technical_details:
Hi --

I believe I've found two vulnerabilities in FreeBSD that can be

chained together to yield privilege escalation from nobody to full

kernel control.

I used an LLM to find both of these bugs, but I validated the bugs

myself and wrote this email and believe everything in it to be

correct. I've validated the bugs on a fresh machine with the attached

PoCs.

The first bug is a use-after-free. The TIOCNOTTY ioctl handler,

tty_drop_ctty() in sys/kern/tty.c, detaches the calling process from

its controlling terminal. It clears the session-to-tty pointers

(s_ttyp, s_ttyvp, s_ttydp) and decrements the tty's session reference

count, but it does not clear the tty-to-session pointer, tp->t_session.

Normally that pointer is cleared later by tty_rel_sess(), which

sess_release() calls when the session's refcount hits zero. But

sess_release() only calls tty_rel_sess() if s_ttyp is still set,

and tty_drop_ctty() just cleared it. So when the last reference to

the session drops and the struct is freed, tp->t_session remains

pointing into freed heap. Any later code path that reads

tp->t_session->s_leader (there are several) is a controlled-deref

primitive.

I've attached a PoC that reproduces this crash.

The second bug is a page-table-walk type confusion. When a process

maps a 1GB superpage (via shm_open2 with SHM_LARGEPAGE), the hardware

mapping for it is a PDPE (a third-level page table entry) with both

the Present bit and the Page Size bit set. The Page Size bit is what

distinguishes "this PDPE is a terminal 1GB mapping" from "this PDPE

points at a page directory." pmap_pkru_update_range() in

sys/amd64/amd64/pmap.c walks a process's page tables to update the

protection-key bits on a range of mappings. For the PDPE level, it

checks the Present bit but not the Page Size bit, and falls through

to pmap_pdpe_to_pde(), which interprets the PDPE's physical-address

field as a pointer to a page directory. For a 1GB superpage, that

physical-address field is the base of the 1GB of userspace data the

process just mapped. The kernel proceeds to read that gigabyte of

user-controlled memory as page table entries, and for every entry with

the Present bit set, rewrites its protection-key bits in place. That

"entry" can be made to live at any physical address the attacker

chooses via the fake PDE's frame-number field — the kernel thinks

it's updating a page table page, but the target can be anything in

RAM.

I've attached a second PoC that reproduces this crash.

Neither bug requires any elevated capability to trigger. TIOCNOTTY is

available to any process with a tty. shm_open2 with SHM_LARGEPAGE and

the sysarch(AMD64_SET_PKRU) call that reaches pmap_pkru_update_range

are both permitted under default resource limits and are explicitly

whitelisted under Capsicum. The pmap_pkru path, though, does require

that the CPU has Protection Keys; any Intel CPU since Skylake or AMD

since Zen 3 should qualify.

I've also attached two PoCs that, when run as nobody on a stock

FreeBSD build, each demonstrate uid=0 access:

- The first PoC chains both bugs: the UAF for a control-flow hijack,

  and the type confusion as an address oracle. It needs a CPU with

  Protection Keys (Skylake+/Zen 3+), ~4GB free RAM for a 1GB

  contiguous allocation, and at least two CPUs for a race.

- The second PoC uses only the UAF, but it needs a nobody-

  writable tmpfs mount, which isn't default.

Both PoCs give an unprivileged local process root on 14.4-RELEASE

GENERIC amd64.

first. A malicious process creates a new session (with setsid) to

open the slave side of a pseudo-terminal, makes that tty its

controlling terminal (TIOCSCTTY), then immediately disowns it with

(TIOCNOTTY). When that process exits, its session is freed. The pty's

t_session is now a stale pointer. Closing the pty master triggers

tty_rel_gone, then ttydisc_modem, and then tty_signal_sessleader,

which runs the following code:

    // sys/kern/tty.c, tty_signal_sessleader()

    if (tp->t_session != NULL && tp->t_session->s_leader != NULL) {

        p = tp->t_session->s_leader;   // freed heap, offset 8

        PROC_LOCK(p);                   //   lock cmpxchg on p+0x140

        kern_psignal(p, sig);

        PROC_UNLOCK(p);

    }

kern_psignal calls tdsendsignal, which, after only a zombie-state

check, calls knote() on p->p_klist. knote() walks the list and for

each entry calls kn->kn_fop->f_event(kn, hint). If the freed session

slot has been refilled such that s_leader points at attacker-controlled

memory, there's a direct path from PROC_LOCK to an indirect call with

a controlled function pointer, with the first argument pointing into

attacker controlled memory.

The first PoC works by taking this write, and using it to stack pivot

and then ROPing its way to code execution in the kernel.

The pmap bug can help make this exploit simpler. The vulnerable

code is as follows:

    // sys/amd64/amd64/pmap.c, pmap_pkru_update_range()

    pdpe = pmap_pml4e_to_pdpe(pml4e, va);

    if ((*pdpe & X86_PG_V) == 0) {            // checks Present

        ... continue;                          //   does NOT check PG_PS

    }

    ...

    pde = pmap_pdpe_to_pde(pdpe, va);         // treats PDPE as PD pointer

    ptpaddr = *pde;                            //   *pde is inside the 1GB page

    ...

    if ((ptpaddr & PG_PS) != 0) {             // checks PG_PS here, one

        ...                                    //   level too late

    }

    ...

    for (ptep = pmap_pde_to_pte(pde, va); ... ) {

        pte = *ptep;

        if ((pte & X86_PG_V) == 0) continue;  // user data, bit 0 decides

        newpte = (pte & ~X86_PG_PKU_MASK) | X86_PG_PKU(keyidx);

        *ptep = newpte;                        // writes bits [62:59]

    }

The PDE-level PG_PS check is correct; it's the PDPE-level check

that's missing. With a 1GB mapping at the right virtual address, a

sysarch(AMD64_SET_PKRU) call on a 4KB range inside that mapping

will read a quadword the attacker wrote at a chosen offset in the

1GB page as a "PDE," follow its physical-address bits to any physical

page in the machine, and then read and modify quadwords in that

physical page as "PTEs."

The write primitive itself (bits [62:59] of any odd quadword in

physical RAM) is awkward to exploit directly. What makes this bug

useful here is not the write itself but what you can learn from

where it lands: point the fake PDE at successive candidate

1GB-aligned physical addresses, put a distinctive sentinel at offset

zero of the 1GB page, fire the sysarch, and then check if the

sentinel's protection-key bits changed. When they do, you've found

the physical address of your own 1GB page, and the kernel virtual

address is just DMAP_MIN_ADDRESS ORed with that physical address.

You now have a gigabyte of attacker-controlled memory at a known

kernel virtual address, which is exactly what the tty bug's exploit

chain needs.

Two proofs of concept are attached. Both run as nobody, both end with

root reading /etc/master.passwd. They differ only in how they solve

the "known kernel address of controlled memory" problem.

I've provided additional descriptions of the PoCs at the end of this

email; they're not important in order to understand the bug but I've

provided them in case you're curious. I spent less time validating the

LLM's claims here so there may be some errors.

There's a relatively simple fix for both bugs. For the tty one, the

one-line version is to clear tp->t_session in tty_drop_ctty after

dropping the session lock but while still holding the tty lock:

--- sys/kern/tty.c

+++ sys/kern/tty.c

@@ tty_drop_ctty @@

  session->s_ttyp = NULL;

  session->s_ttyvp = NULL;

  session->s_ttydp = NULL;

  SESS_UNLOCK(session);

+ tp->t_session = NULL;

  tp->t_sessioncnt--;

  p->p_flag &= ~P_CONTROLT;

I think this is what tty_rel_sess() would have done, had

sess_release() reached it.

For the pmap bug, I'm less sure what to do. I think that it should

work to check PG_PS on the PDPE the same way the function already

does for the PDE one level down, but I'm out of my depth in my

systems knowledge here and may be misunderstanding things;

nevertheless, here's a patch that does stop this exploit on my

machine:

--- sys/amd64/amd64/pmap.c

+++ sys/amd64/amd64/pmap.c

@@ pmap_pkru_update_range @@

  pdpe = pmap_pml4e_to_pdpe(pml4e, va);

  if ((*pdpe & X86_PG_V) == 0) {

  va_next = (va + NBPDP) & ~PDPMASK;

  if (va_next < va)

  va_next = eva;

  continue;

  }

+ if ((*pdpe & PG_PS) != 0) {

+ va_next = (va + NBPDP) & ~PDPMASK;

+ if (va_next < va)

+ va_next = eva;

+ newpde = (*pdpe & ~X86_PG_PKU_MASK) | X86_PG_PKU(keyidx);

+ if (newpde != *pdpe) {

+ *pdpe = newpde;

+ changed = true;

+ }

+ continue;

+ }

Both bugs were introduced in 2019 if my sleuthing is correct. The tty

bug was introduced in 1b50b999f9b5 (2019-11-30, the commit that

implemented TIOCNOTTY), and the pmap bug in e7a9df16e65 (2019-02-20,

the commit that added PKU support). I've checked both are still

present on main and releng/15.0.

Happy to provide more detail, or answer any other questions.

Nicholas

Additional details on the PoCs:

lpe.c uses no second bug. The KERN_PROC_PID sysctl (available to any

user on their own processes) returns several raw kernel pointers in

struct kinfo_proc — ki_paddr is the process's own struct proc*,

ki_args is its struct pargs*. struct pargs is the process's argv as a

contiguous buffer, allocated from general malloc with a size controlled

by the argv length. Fork children with ~240-byte argv strings, and each

child's pargs lands in the malloc-256 bucket at an address the parent

can read via sysctl. On a quiet system these allocations are adjacent

at a 256-byte stride. The exploit tiles its fake kernel structures

(the fake proc, knlist, knote, filterops and the ROP stack) across

seven such adjacent slots, encoding the bytes as the argv strings

themselves. Every internal pointer in the fake structures is computed

from addresses leaked via sysctl from the exploit's own children. The

placement is made deterministic with a relay-execve technique: each

child first holds a dummy slot, then reads the real payload from a

pipe and re-execs itself, so the free of the old pargs and the alloc

of the new one happen inside a single execve syscall and hit the same

per-CPU allocator slot. The 128-byte session refill (for the dangling

tp->t_session) uses bind() on an AF_UNIX socket with a sockaddr_un

sized to land in malloc-128; this needs a tmpfs mount — the UFS

softdep worklist structures (dirrem, bmsafemap, diradd) share

malloc-128 and overwrite the slot between the bind and the trigger.

unified_exploit.c uses the pmap_pkru bug as the address oracle. The

1GB page's self-probed DMAP address is the "known kernel VA," and the

fake structures are built in the first few kilobytes of that page.

The session refill is done by racing close(pty_master) against a

bind() spammer thread: sys_bind's getsockaddr malloc is transient

(freed before bind returns), but it's live for the whole of

uipc_bindat's namei and VOP_CREATE. On a two-CPU system, pin the

bind spammer to the CPU whose per-CPU cache the freed session went to,

close the pty from the other CPU, and the read of tp->t_session lands

inside one of the spammer's transient windows. No tmpfs needed, but

the race window is narrow on real hardware.

To be very explicit about the tty trigger, since both PoCs share it:

  1. posix_openpt() → master fd, ptsname/open → slave fd.

  2. Clear CLOCAL on the slave (else ttydisc_modem short-circuits

     and never reaches tty_signal_sessleader).

  3. Fork. Child: setsid(), open the slave again, ioctl(TIOCSCTTY)

     to make it controlling, ioctl(TIOCNOTTY) to drop it, _exit(0).

  4. tty_drop_ctty clears the session's s_ttyp. Child's exit drops

     the last session ref. sess_release sees s_ttyp==NULL, skips

     tty_rel_sess. Session freed. tp->t_session dangling.

  5. Parent: fill the freed malloc-128 slot (either PoC's method).

  6. Parent: close the master fd. ttydev_close → tty_rel_gone →

     ttydisc_modem(tp, 0) → tty_signal_sessleader(tp, SIGHUP) →

     tp->t_session->s_leader → attacker pointer → PROC_LOCK →

     kern_psignal → tdsendsignal → knote(p->p_klist, ...) → pivot.

To be very explicit about the pmap_pkru trigger:

  1. shm_open2(SHM_ANON, ..., SHM_LARGEPAGE) with lp_psind=2 (1GB).

  2. ftruncate to 1GB, mmap at a 1GB-aligned userspace VA.

  3. In the 1GB page at the byte offsets the kernel will read as

     page table indices: write a fake PDE at offset (outer_idx * 8)

     with X86_PG_V set and a candidate physical address in the

     frame-number bits. Write a sentinel at offset (inner_idx * 8)

     with X86_PG_V set.

  4. sysarch(AMD64_SET_PKRU) on a 4KB range at 1g_va + delta, where

     delta encodes the outer_idx and inner_idx in the normal

     vaddr-to-pagetable-index bitfields.

  5. The kernel reads your 1GB page as a PD, reads your fake PDE,

     follows it to the candidate physical page, reads and rewrites

     quadwords there.

  6. If the candidate physical page is your own 1GB page, the

     sentinel at offset (inner_idx * 8) has its bits [62:59]

     rewritten. Check it from userspace. If it changed, that

     candidate is your physical address.
title: Local privilege escalation via tty_drop_ctty t_session UAF + pmap_pkru_update_range PDPE walk
